neurotransmission, usually high serum and
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) titers of anti-GAD anti-
bodies and more rarely antibodies against
the glycine alpha1 receptor, or the gamma-
aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor–associated
protein.1,2,5 Antiamphiphysin, antigephyrin, and
anti-Ri antibodies are characteristic of the para-
neoplastic SPS form. 1,6 Association with HLA
DQB1*0201 and diabetes mellitus type 1 in-
creases the basis for an autoimmune etiology.
Symptomatic therapy (such as baclofen, dantro-
lene, diazepam, clonazepam, etc.) often offers
partial response.2 Although therapeutic success
had been reported with the use of plasma
exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin
(IVIg), most patients continue to follow a relent-
less course.2,6 Rituximab and other cytotoxic
agents are potential therapeutic options. 2,6–8
Although the spectrum of anti-GAD antibody
syndrome is characterized by heterogeneous
clinical manifestations and responses to imuno-
modulator therapies, we report 2 cases with
unique features at the disease presentation.

betes mellitus type I and dyslipidemia pre-
sented with 2 months of hiccups and recent
sudden-onset difficulty urinating requiring
continuous urinary catheterization, associated

with abdominal cramps, nausea, tenesmus,
constipation, and vertigo. Sitting or standing
up induced abnormal sweating, emesis, and
light-headedness. He had a severe feeling of
rectal pressure and was unable to have bowel
movement without pain. In the ensuing weeks,
he developed movement-induced spasms in
the feet and calves, impairing ambulation. CSF
studies revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis.
Brain and entire spine MR imaging was
unremarkable. Patient was transferred to our
medical center because of progressive debili-
tating symptoms. Our examination showed
intermittent hiccups, spastic tone and hyper-
reflexia in the lower extremities, sustained
knee and ankle clonus, high-stepping gait, and
increased rectal tone. Direction-changing nys-
tagmus was noticed intermittently. Patient also
experienced horizontal diplopia due to the left
sixth nerve palsy for 1 week. There were
neither other cranial nerves affected nor
sensory abnormalities. Mental status was main-
tained throughout. Gastrointestinal consulta-
tion revealed clinical evidence for delayed
gastric emptying and bowel retention with
hyperactive anal sphincter. Anal manometry
could not be performed because of severe
spasms and discomfort. Urinary sphincter
tightness impeded regular urinary catheteri-
zation and the need of 18F Coude catheter.
Serum GAD65 antibody was 1.54 nmol/L
(reference range #0.02 nmol/L). CSF studies
remained unremarkable, including anti-GAD65
antibody and paraneoplastic profile. Serum am-
phiphysin antibody was negative. Electromyog-
raphy and nerve conduction studies of lower
extremities were unremarkable.
High doses of diazepam and baclofen
and IVIg had no benefit. With plasma
exchange, the limb spasticity mildly
improved, but the tight urethral sphincter,
abdominal cramps, and tenesmus persisted.
He was bedbound because of the spasms
and was losing weight because of difficulties
with feeding despite these therapies. The
patient had a dramatic response to rituximab
infusion at 1000 mg given while he was in
the hospital. Because of insurance limita-
tions, he only received that treatment and
was continued on weekly plasma exchanges
and high doses of diazepam and baclofen.
Ambulation, urinary retention, and gastroin-
testinal symptoms resolved after 4 weeks. He
had repeat rituximab 8 months after the initial
treatment and then 6 months after that. By 8
months, all the symptoms resolved and all
treatments except rituximab were discontin-
ued. Anti-GAD antibody titers have remained
persistently elevated ( .30 units/mL) despite
complete resolution of symptoms. He has
been able to do long distance running now,
14 months after the third and last rituximab
infusion.

Case 2
Forty-four-year-old man with medical his-
tory of obstructive sleep apnea presented with
intermittent urinary retention and constipation
for approximately 2 months, followed by pro-
gressive cramping and spasms in the lower
extremities that were triggered by startle, stress,
loud noises, and tactile stimulation. Initial
symptoms started 2 weeks after influenza
vaccination. On examination, increased tone
and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities were
accompanied by spastic gait and toe walking.
Symptoms progressed to a wheelchair-bound
state, complicated by severe constipation. The
urologist determined the need for suprapubic
bladder catheterization for urinary retention
management. In addition, patient experienced
2 self-limiting episodes of diplopia and was
diagnosed with fourth and, respectively, sixth
nerves palsies. Serum anti-GAD65 antibody titer
was highly elevated at 250 units/mL, and anti-
bodies to pancreatic islet cells were found
elevated as well. Serologic workup for infec-
tions, autoimmune and paraneoplastic condi-
tions, brain and spine MR imaging, CT chest,
abdomen, and pelvis was unrevealing. Esopha-
geal manometry revealed a prolonged refrac-
tory phase of esophageal peristalsis and
abnormal relaxation of the lower and upper
esophageal sphincters. The high-resolution ano-
rectal manometry interpretation was consistent
with outlet obstruction because internal anal
sphincter did not relax with balloon distension
during normal values and sensation of the urge

to defecate was felt at lower volumes (100 mL)
than normal (120 mL). In addition, elevated
maximum resting sphincter pressure (117 mm
Hg in our case, with normal value being less
than 98 mm Hg) and maximum sphincter
squeeze pressure (323 mm Hg in our case
compared with normal less than 254 mm Hg)
were observed. Urinary retention and consti-
pation resolved after 2 months of IVIg therapy.
Lower extremity spasms and gait impairment
improved with IVIg, baclofen, and diazepam;
maintenance therapy was required to assure
fully ambulatory state, return to full-time job,
and cardio exercises.
DISCUSSION
The Dalakas diagnostic criteria for typical
SPS are based on clinical symptoms and signs
(axial stiffness, superimposed painful spasms,
absent neurological or cognitive impairment
that could explain the stiffness, and response
to diazepam), serologic (positive anti-GAD65
or amphiphysin antibodies), and electrodiag-
nostic markers (continuous motor unit activity
in agonist and antagonist muscles).9
Although our cases did not have evi-
dence of electrodiagnostic markers of SPS, they
otherwise had very characteristic clinical and
serologic findings. Both cases bring distinctive
clinical presentation of SPS with anorectal
spasms, gastrointestinal outlet obstruction, ure-
thral sphincter spasticity, and signs of brain-
stem dysfunction. Despite somewhat similar
initial presentation, they exhibited dissimilar
response to immunomodulating therapies.
To our knowledge, increased urinary and
gastrointestinal sphincter tone and spasticity,
requiring urethral catheterization and even
suprapubic bladder catheterization and serial
enemas, have not been described in the
literature as presenting signs of the SPS.
Sphincter muscle spasms manifested by uri-
nary retention and anal hypertonia were the
preliminary warning signs. Intractable hiccups
and abdominal cramps, likely induced by the
diaphragmatic and abdominal muscle spasms
also preceded the limb-associated symptoms in
case 1. In addition, emesis although to be
secondary to gastric outlet syndrome was
a prominent early symptom. Lower extrem-
ity spasms, clonus, and rigidity followed the
sphincter-related symptoms, at different
time intervals, couple weeks in the first case
and 2 months in the second case.
Spinal cord and extrapyramidal signs
associated with SPS were reported previously
by Pittock et al. 10 In those cases, 4,11 the limb
symptoms were initially manifested, and there
was a delay of few years between limb symp-
toms and sphincter involvement. The sphincter
disturbances described were urinary frequency,
urgency, and occasional urge incontinence.11
Urodynamic studies were not performed
in our patients despite obtaining urological
consultations. The urologists felt confident in
both cases that the tightness of the urethral
sphincter caused urinary retention based on
extremely difficult catheterization, and therefore
advanced catheterization techniques were
applied. Esophageal and anorectal manometry
were completed in case 2. Abnormal relaxation
of the upper and lower esophageal sphincters,
prolonged refractory phase for the peristalsis,
a n o m a l o u sr e l a x a t i o no ft h ei n t e r n a la n a ls p h i n c -
ter, abnormal maximum resting, and squeezing
pressures of the anal sphincter provided objec-
tive evidence for gastrointestinal outlet obstruc-
tion. Manometry studies were not repeated after
immunomodulation therapies, given symptoms
resolved completely. Based on the observed
internal anal sphincter abnormalities, autonomic
nervous system involvement is implicated in this
presentation. Orthostatic symptoms and sweat-
ing could be potentially explained by dysauto-
nomia as well. However, skeletal muscle
sphincters seem to be affected as well, and it
is not possible to determine the relative impact
of each of these mechanisms. The same patho-
physiologic mechanism of anti-GAD antibody
syndrome is likely responsible for the skeletal
sphincters spasms and rigidity.
Notwithstanding lack of controlled clin-
ical trials, adult and pediatric SPS cases with
successful response to rituximab have been
reported.6,12–14 Rituximab was initiated in
those cases based on increased disease sever-
ity and lacking response to other immune

modulatory agents, and induced a lasting clin-
ical remission.6 At least 2 doses each of 500
mg/m2 infusion spaced over 14 days have re-
sulted in symptomatic improvement.13 Further
rituximab dosing spaced 6 to 8 months was
reported in relapsing cases. 15 Rituximab 1000
mg infusions proved to be a good therapeutic
option in our first patient, after failing the
more traditional therapies (baclofen, benzodia-
zepines, IVIg, and plasma exchange). The
patient required a total of 3 infusions, spaced
8 and then 6 months apart due to insurance
barriers. Persistent elevation of anti-GAD65
antibodies despite successful immunotherapy
was seen in our patients and concurs with the
literature reports.7 Serologic monitoring is not
recommended, and the optimal therapy dura-
tion is unclear. 16 Case 2 had recurrence of
symptoms with discontinuing IVIg and has re-
mained on it. Case 1 has not required further
rituximab for 14 months.
We want to raise awareness that the
initial manifestation of SPS can be gastrointesti-
nal and/or genitourinary sphincter dysfunction,
before the limb or truncal symptomatology. A
clue to the urethral sphincter spasm is the
difficulty in urinary catheterization. The tenes-
mus is a clue to the anorectal spasm. Dysauto-
nomia is part of the spectrum of manifestations
of anti-GAD antibody syndrome, including sub-
types of SPS, cerebellar ataxia, and epilepsy.
Further research into the elucidation of the
mechanism involved and potential therapies
targeting autonomic nervous system dysfunc-
tion should be contemplated.
